title: Procedural impropriety
subtitle: The fairness checklist: hearing, reasons, consultation and bias
objectives: Explain why Ridge v Baldwin abolished the old requirement that a function be 'judicial' before natural justice could apply
State when the common law imposes a duty to give reasons, and identify the interests that duty protects
Apply the apparent bias test from Porter v Magill to a fact pattern involving a decision-maker with a personal or professional connection to the outcome
Work through a multi-issue fair-hearing problem the way an examiner will present one: several procedural defects stacked in a single fact pattern

leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes that natural justice applies wherever a decision seriously affects someone's rights or interests, not only to bodies exercising a 'judicial' function

leadingAuthorities.citation: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Doody [1994] 1 AC 531
leadingAuthorities.role: Source of the modern common law duty to give reasons in appropriate cases

leadingAuthorities.citation: R v Bow Street Metropolitan Stipendiary Magistrate, ex p Pinochet Ugarte (No 2) [2000] 1 AC 119
leadingAuthorities.role: Automatic disqualification for a decision-maker with a direct, non-pecuniary interest in the outcome
States the modern test for apparent bias: the fair-minded and informed observer
Expands the right to an oral hearing and reframes procedural fairness as valuable in itself, not only as a means to a correct outcome

leadingAuthorities.citation: R (Moseley) v Haringey London Borough Council [2014] UKSC 56
leadingAuthorities.role: Sets the common law standard for a fair consultation exercise

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students learn the four heads of procedural impropriety — hearing, reasons, consultation, bias — as an unordered list to recite. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know all four heads. This lesson is about running them against a fact pattern like a checklist, in the order that finds every defect, not just the first one.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on naming the tests here before. The test pool below leans towards application: expect layered fact patterns with more than one procedural problem hiding in them.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and get the four checklist items solid before moving on — the later parts assume you can name the test for bias, reasons and consultation without hesitation.

overview.hook: A decision can be entirely correct on the merits and still be unlawful. That sentence unsettles most students the first time they hear it, because it means the law sometimes cares more about how a decision was reached than about whether it was right. This lesson gives you a working checklist for that 'how': was there a fair hearing, were reasons given, was consultation genuine, and was the decision-maker free of bias. Run the checklist on any fact pattern, in order, and you will rarely miss the issue an examiner has planted.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 1 September 2026. This is a well-settled area of administrative law common law doctrine; no pending legislative change affects it.

parts.heading: Checklist item one: the right to be heard, and the trap the courts fell into first
parts.voice: checklist-narrative — opens the procedural checklist and immediately shows how an old, wrong way of applying it failed a real claimant
body: Start building the checklist here: does the affected person get to put their case before the decision is made? That sounds obvious. It wasn't, for most of the twentieth century, because courts had convinced themselves that this right — natural justice, or the audi alteram partem rule, 'hear the other side' — only applied to bodies exercising a specifically 'judicial' or 'quasi-judicial' function. An administrative decision, however serious its consequences, supposedly fell outside natural justice altogether.

Ridge v Baldwin is the case that dismantled that distinction. Ridge, the Chief Constable of Brighton, was prosecuted for conspiracy alongside other officers and acquitted — but the trial judge made critical remarks about his leadership. The borough's Watch Committee, exercising its statutory power to dismiss a chief constable for misconduct or unfitness, dismissed him without ever telling him the case against him or giving him a chance to respond.

The House of Lords held the dismissal void. The old 'judicial function' gatekeeping was wrong: what matters is not how the decision-maker is labelled, but the seriousness of what is at stake for the individual — here, a career and a pension built over decades, taken away without so much as a hearing. Ridge v Baldwin is the reason your checklist's first item applies broadly across administrative decision-making today, not just to tribunals dressed up to look like courts.

components.definition: 'Hear the other side' — the natural justice principle that a person facing a decision seriously affecting their rights or interests must be told the case against them and given a fair opportunity to respond before the decision is made.

components.factsShort: A Chief Constable, acquitted of conspiracy but criticised by the trial judge, was dismissed by the Watch Committee without being told the case against him or given a hearing.
components.ratioShort: Natural justice applies wherever a decision seriously affects a person's rights or interests, regardless of whether the decision-maker's function is labelled 'judicial'.

expanded.facts: Ridge was prosecuted for conspiracy to obstruct the course of justice alongside two other officers. He was acquitted, but the trial judge criticised his leadership of the force. Brighton's Watch Committee, acting under statutory powers to dismiss a chief constable, dismissed him for neglect of duty without giving him notice of the charge against him or an opportunity to be heard in his own defence.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Reid held that the previous restriction of natural justice to bodies exercising 'judicial' or 'quasi-judicial' functions was a misreading of earlier authority. The real question is whether the decision seriously affects the rights or interests of the person concerned — here, dismissal from an office with pension consequences plainly did. On that basis the Watch Committee was bound to inform Ridge of the case against him and hear his response before dismissing him; failing to do so rendered the dismissal void.
expanded.significance: Ridge v Baldwin is the foundational modern case for the reach of natural justice in administrative law. It is the reason the fair hearing requirement now applies broadly across disciplinary, regulatory and administrative decision-making, and not only to bodies that look and act like courts.

interaction.prompt: Before Ridge v Baldwin, why did some courts hold that natural justice did not apply to the Watch Committee's dismissal of a chief constable?
options: Because dismissing a chief constable was thought to be an 'administrative' function, not a 'judicial' or 'quasi-judicial' one, and natural justice was wrongly thought to attach only to the latter
Because chief constables have no legal rights at all
Because the Watch Committee had no power to dismiss anyone
interaction.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers overstate the old position — it wasn't that Ridge had no rights, or that the Committee had no power; it was a narrower, now-discredited classification error about which functions attracted natural justice at all.

parts.heading: Checklist item two: reasons
parts.voice: structural — sets out when the duty to give reasons arises as a factor-based test, not an absolute rule
body: The second checklist item: did the decision-maker explain why? English law has never adopted a single, universal duty to give reasons for every administrative decision — but it has, through ex p Doody, recognised a common law duty in appropriate circumstances, built around fairness rather than a blanket rule.

Doody concerned mandatory life sentence prisoners who were not told why the Home Secretary had set their minimum term (the 'tariff') at a particular length, or given the judiciary's own recommended tariff for comparison. The House of Lords held that fairness required reasons here: without them, a prisoner facing a decision of this severity, with genuinely no other way to know whether an error had crept into the process, could not meaningfully challenge it. Reasons are what make the earlier checklist item — the right to be heard — actually worth something after the fact: you can't identify whether a decision was wrong, or even challenge it, if you're never told why it was made.

The factors from Doody and later cases cluster around a few recurring themes: how severe the consequences are for the individual: is there a right of appeal that depends on knowing the reasoning; is the decision otherwise 'inscrutable' — impossible to make sense of without an explanation; and whether reasons would reveal something the decision-maker has a legitimate interest in withholding. None of these factors is individually decisive — the duty to give reasons is generated by weighing them together, not read off a fixed statutory list.

components.label: Factors pointing towards a common law duty to give reasons
points: Severity of the consequences for the individual (liberty, livelihood, reputation)
Whether a right of appeal or further challenge depends on knowing the reasoning
Whether the decision is otherwise 'inscrutable' — impossible to assess without an explanation
The absence of any legitimate reason (e.g. national security, commercial confidentiality) for withholding reasons

interaction.prompt: Which statement best describes the common law duty to give reasons after ex p Doody?
options: There is a single, universal duty to give reasons for every public law decision, without exception
There is no duty to give reasons in English administrative law
Whether reasons are required depends on a fairness-based weighing of factors such as the severity of consequences and whether the decision would otherwise be inscrutable
interaction.briefExplanation: Doody is a context-sensitive fairness case, not a universal rule. It generates a duty in appropriate circumstances rather than imposing one across the board.

parts.heading: Checklist item three: bias — actual, and the fair-minded observer
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells two stories, one of undisclosed connection and one of the test that followed
body: Third item: was the decision-maker free of bias? Start with the starkest version. In R v Bow Street Metropolitan Stipendiary Magistrate, ex p Pinochet Ugarte (No 2), the House of Lords had to reconsider its own earlier ruling on General Pinochet's extradition after it emerged that one of the Law Lords who decided it, Lord Hoffmann, was an unpaid director of a charitable arm of Amnesty International — an organisation that had been given permission to intervene in the case and had campaigned actively against Pinochet. Lord Hoffmann had no financial interest at all. The House of Lords still set aside its own earlier decision.

Pinochet (No 2) establishes automatic disqualification: where a judge has a personal, non-pecuniary interest in the outcome closely linked to a party or cause in the case — not just money, but a role that puts the judge's own object in promoting the same cause as one side — the decision is void without any need to ask whether the judge was actually influenced. The appearance of a structural conflict is enough.

Most bias cases aren't this stark, which is where Porter v Magill supplies the general test. Dame Shirley Porter, leader of Westminster City Council, had been found by an auditor to have engaged in unlawful gerrymandering — selling council homes to likely Conservative voters to affect election outcomes. Part of her challenge concerned whether the auditor's earlier public comments about the case showed apparent bias. The House of Lords restated the governing test: would a fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, conclude that there was a real possibility the tribunal was biased? Notice what the test does not ask — it doesn't require proof the decision-maker was actually swayed, and it doesn't ask whether the decision-maker themselves felt biased. It asks what a sensible, informed outsider would conclude about the risk.

components.factsShort: Westminster's council leader was found to have engaged in unlawful gerrymandering; part of her challenge concerned whether the auditor's conduct of the case showed apparent bias.
components.ratioShort: Apparent bias is tested by asking whether a fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude there was a real possibility the decision-maker was biased.

expanded.facts: Dame Shirley Porter, as leader of Westminster City Council, was found by the district auditor to have deliberately designated certain council estates for sale to owner-occupiers, rather than continuing as social housing, with the object of increasing the number of likely Conservative voters in marginal wards ahead of local elections — a policy that became known as 'homes for votes'. Among other grounds, the case examined the standard for apparent bias in the conduct of the auditor's inquiry.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Hope, reviewing the earlier, more claimant-unfriendly formulations of the bias test, restated it as: the court must first ascertain all the circumstances which have a bearing on the suggestion that the decision-maker was biased, and then ask whether those circumstances would lead a fair-minded and informed observer to conclude that there was a real possibility, or a real danger, that the tribunal was biased.
expanded.significance: This is now the standard test for apparent bias across English public law, replacing earlier, more fragmented formulations. It sets an objective standard judged from the perspective of a hypothetical informed observer, not the parties, and not the decision-maker's own self-assessment.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence stating the Porter v Magill test for apparent bias.
interaction.passage: The court must first ascertain all the circumstances which have a bearing on the suggestion that the judge was biased. It must then ask whether those circumstances would lead a fair-minded and informed observer to conclude that there was a real possibility, or a real danger, that the tribunal was biased. This is an objective test, judged from the standpoint of the hypothetical observer, not the parties themselves.
interaction.ratioSentence: It must then ask whether those circumstances would lead a fair-minded and informed observer to conclude that there was a real possibility, or a real danger, that the tribunal was biased.

parts.heading: Checklist item four: consultation, and a fifth item hiding inside it — the oral hearing
parts.voice: case-narrative — applies two related fairness cases through a worked scenario
body: Consultation is where the checklist meets a practical question: if a public body chooses to consult before deciding, how fair does that consultation have to be? R (Moseley) v Haringey London Borough Council answers this for a council's consultation on changes to its council tax reduction scheme, which affected some of the borough's poorest residents. The council consulted on one option — reducing the scheme's generosity — without properly explaining the realistic alternatives it had considered and rejected, such as making savings elsewhere in its budget.

The Supreme Court held the consultation was unlawful. Fair consultation, building on long-standing Sedley/Gunning-style principles, requires that consultees be given sufficient information — including about realistic alternatives — to make an intelligent response, and that responses genuinely be considered before a final decision, not merely collected as a formality. A consultation that presents only the preferred option, dressed up as a genuine choice, fails this standard.

A related but distinct fairness question is whether an affected person is entitled to an oral hearing, rather than only a chance to make written representations. R (Osborn) v Parole Board addressed this for prisoners facing parole and recall decisions. The Supreme Court held that oral hearings should be held more often than the Parole Board's previous practice allowed, wherever there is a disputed issue of fact, wherever an oral hearing would genuinely help assess risk, or wherever it is otherwise needed for a fair, transparent process. Lord Reed's judgment is notable for treating fairness as valuable for its own sake — participation and dignity, not only as an instrument for reaching a more accurate result — a point worth remembering whenever an exam question asks you to justify why a procedural safeguard matters even if the outcome would probably have been the same.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that as long as a public body technically 'consulted' — sent out a document and collected responses — the consultation must be lawful.
components.whyItsWrong: Moseley shows the form of consultation isn't enough. If the material presented to consultees is skewed towards a single preferred outcome, or realistic alternatives are omitted, the exercise fails the fairness standard even though a consultation, in name, took place.

interaction.prompt: A council consults residents on cutting a bus subsidy, presenting only the cut as an option and not mentioning that it had also considered, and rejected, raising parking charges instead. Applying Moseley, is this consultation likely to be lawful?
options: No — fair consultation requires disclosing realistic alternatives considered, not just the preferred option
Yes — any consultation exercise, however framed, satisfies the legal duty to consult
Yes, provided the council genuinely reads the responses it receives, regardless of what information was given
interaction.explanation: Moseley requires that consultees be given enough information, including about realistic alternatives, to make an intelligent response. Omitting an alternative the council itself considered and rejected mirrors the flaw that made the Haringey consultation unlawful.

parts.heading: Running the full checklist
parts.voice: checklist-narrative — walks through a single dense fact pattern issue by issue, the way an exam question will present one
body: Examiners rarely test one procedural head in isolation. A well-built problem question stacks two or three checklist items into a single fact pattern, and the skill this lesson is really building is running the checklist methodically rather than spotting only the first issue you recognise.

Take a fact pattern like this: a regulator investigates a doctor for professional misconduct. The panel chair has a personal friendship with the complainant, undisclosed to the doctor. The doctor is given written notice of the allegations but is refused an oral hearing despite disputing the facts. The panel suspends the doctor's licence and gives a one-line decision with no reasoning. Run the checklist: bias (the chair's undisclosed friendship — Porter v Magill, arguably even approaching Pinochet-style automatic disqualification depending on how close the connection is), the right to an oral hearing (Osborn — a disputed factual issue is exactly the circumstance in which an oral hearing should usually be held), and reasons (Doody-style factors: suspension of a licence to practise is severe, any appeal depends on knowing the reasoning, and a one-line decision is inscrutable).

Notice that the checklist items reinforce each other rather than competing for attention: the same fact pattern can breach several heads at once, and a strong answer identifies each breach separately, with its own authority and its own reasoning, rather than folding them into one vague claim that 'the process was unfair'. That precision — naming which head, citing which case, applying which test — is what separates a mid-range answer from a strong one in this area.

components.label: The procedural impropriety checklist
points: 1. Right to be heard — was the affected person told the case against them and given a real chance to respond? (Ridge v Baldwin)
2. Oral hearing — where facts are disputed or oral evidence would help, was one held rather than only written submissions? (Osborn v Parole Board)
3. Reasons — does fairness require an explanation here, weighing severity, appeal rights and inscrutability? (ex p Doody)
4. Consultation — if consultation took place, was it genuine, with realistic alternatives disclosed and responses actually considered? (Moseley v Haringey)

5. Bias — would a fair-minded and informed observer see a real possibility of bias, or does the decision-maker have a direct personal interest triggering automatic disqualification? (Porter v Magill; Pinochet (No 2))

interaction.prompt: A university's academic misconduct panel investigates a student. The panel chair previously supervised the student's dissertation and had a documented dispute with the student over the mark awarded. The student is refused an oral hearing despite disputing the facts. The panel expels the student with a decision stating only 'the allegation is upheld'. Analyse the procedural fairness issues.
factsToOrder: The panel chair previously had a documented dispute with the student
The student disputes the facts but is refused an oral hearing
The panel's decision states only 'the allegation is upheld', with no further reasoning

Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the panel's decision is unlawful for procedural impropriety, on grounds of apparent bias, denial of an oral hearing, and failure to give reasons.
modelAnswer.rule: Apparent bias is tested by asking whether a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias (Porter v Magill). An oral hearing should generally be held where facts are genuinely disputed and an oral hearing would assist a fair assessment (Osborn v Parole Board). A common law duty to give reasons arises where fairness requires it, weighing the severity of consequences, the existence of any further challenge, and whether the decision would otherwise be inscrutable (ex p Doody).
modelAnswer.application: The chair's documented prior dispute with the student over a mark is exactly the kind of connection a fair-minded and informed observer would treat as raising a real possibility of bias — this is not a fanciful or trivial link. The refusal of an oral hearing, despite a genuine factual dispute, falls short of Osborn's standard, since oral evidence would plainly assist the panel in resolving that dispute fairly. Finally, expulsion is a severe consequence, any onward challenge depends on understanding the panel's reasoning, and a one-line 'the allegation is upheld' decision is inscrutable in exactly the sense Doody identifies.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The decision is vulnerable to challenge on three separate but reinforcing grounds — apparent bias, denial of a needed oral hearing, and failure to give adequate reasons — any one of which is likely sufficient on its own to render the process unfair.

testPool.prompt: State the modern test for apparent bias.
acceptableAnswers: fair-minded and informed observer, real possibility of bias
whether a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias
testPool.modelAnswer: Whether a fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that there was a real possibility that the tribunal was biased (Porter v Magill).

testPool.prompt: Did Ridge v Baldwin hold that natural justice only applies to bodies exercising a 'judicial' function?
options: No — it rejected that narrow classification and applied natural justice wherever a decision seriously affects someone's rights or interests
Yes — it confirmed natural justice is limited to judicial functions

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four recognised heads of procedural impropriety covered in this lesson?
options: The right to a fair hearing
The duty to give reasons in appropriate cases
The rule against bias
Whether the decision was the most cost-effective option available
testPool.trapExplanation: Cost-effectiveness is a merits question, not a procedural fairness question — confusing the two is exactly the mistake examiners are testing for when they mix a procedural impropriety problem with irrationality-style facts.

testPool.prompt: Name the case establishing automatic disqualification of a decision-maker with a direct personal, non-pecuniary interest in the outcome.
acceptableAnswers: R v Bow Street Magistrate, ex p Pinochet Ugarte (No 2)
testPool.modelAnswer: R v Bow Street Metropolitan Stipendiary Magistrate, ex p Pinochet Ugarte (No 2) [2000] 1 AC 119.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between apparent bias (Porter v Magill) and automatic disqualification (Pinochet (No 2))?
options: Automatic disqualification applies where the decision-maker has a direct personal interest closely linked to the case, without needing to apply the fair-minded observer test; apparent bias is the broader, more commonly used test for less direct connections
They are the same test with different names
Automatic disqualification has replaced the apparent bias test entirely

testPool.prompt: Put these developments in the order they occurred.
items: Ridge v Baldwin rejects the requirement that a function be 'judicial' for natural justice to apply
R v SSHD, ex p Doody recognises a common law duty to give reasons in appropriate cases
Porter v Magill restates the modern test for apparent bias
R (Osborn) v Parole Board expands the circumstances requiring an oral hearing

testPool.prompt: In the passage below from Osborn v Parole Board, highlight the sentence capturing why oral hearings matter beyond just producing a more accurate outcome.
testPool.passage: The purpose of holding an oral hearing is not confined to assisting the Board to make an accurate decision. It also enables the prisoner to participate in a decision with important implications for them, and to be heard by the person or body deciding their case, in a manner which respects their dignity. Procedural fairness is thus valuable in itself, and not only as a means to a correct result.
testPool.ratioSentence: Procedural fairness is thus valuable in itself, and not only as a means to a correct result.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a public body which consults on a decision, but only ever presents its own preferred option without mentioning realistic alternatives it considered, has satisfied its duty to consult fairly?
sliderLabels: Yes — any consultation that collects responses is lawful
No — Moseley requires realistic alternatives to be disclosed
testPool.correctPosition: No — Moseley requires realistic alternatives to be disclosed
testPool.explanation: R (Moseley) v Haringey LBC requires consultees to be given sufficient information, including about realistic alternatives, to make an intelligent response — presenting only the preferred option fails that standard even if responses are technically collected.

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'Ex p Doody means every public authority must always give reasons for every decision it makes.' What is wrong with this claim?
options: Doody generates a context-sensitive duty depending on factors like severity of consequences and inscrutability, not a universal rule applying to every decision
Nothing is wrong with the claim
Doody actually held that reasons should never be given
testPool.trapExplanation: This overstates Doody into a blanket rule it never was. The duty to give reasons is generated by weighing fairness factors in context, so some decisions — where consequences are minor, or no further challenge depends on the reasoning — will not attract the duty at all.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that most clearly triggers the Ridge v Baldwin right to be heard.
testPool.scenarioText: A regulator investigates a firm for a suspected breach, reviews internal documents, and then issues a formal warning notice to the firm's director without ever informing him of the allegation or inviting any response before deciding to suspend his licence.
tappableSpans: without ever informing him of the allegation or inviting any response
testPool.correctSpan: without ever informing him of the allegation or inviting any response
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the breach. A serious decision — suspending a licence — was made without telling the affected person the case against him or giving him any chance to respond, which is precisely the failure Ridge v Baldwin condemned.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the moment the director is denied any opportunity to know or respond to the case against him, rather than the investigative steps that came before it.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more clearly calls for an oral hearing under the Osborn v Parole Board standard?
testPool.scenarioA: A parole applicant disputes the factual basis of a key risk assessment relied on by the panel, and an oral hearing would help the panel test that disputed evidence.
testPool.scenarioB: A parole applicant accepts all the facts relied on by the panel and challenges only the weight given to settled, undisputed evidence.
testPool.explanation: Osborn ties the case for an oral hearing to genuinely disputed facts and situations where hearing directly from the individual would assist a fair assessment. Where the facts are agreed and only the weighing is contested, the case for an oral hearing over written submissions is far weaker.

testPool.prompt: A disciplinary panel member owns a small number of shares in the company that is a party before the panel. Applying Pinochet (No 2) and Porter v Magill together, what is the most accurate description of the position?
options: A direct financial interest in the outcome can itself trigger automatic disqualification, and even where it does not, it is likely to satisfy the fair-minded and informed observer test for apparent bias
Financial interests are irrelevant to bias unless the member personally benefits from the specific decision
Only non-financial interests, like the one in Pinochet itself, can ever amount to disqualifying bias
testPool.explanation: A pecuniary interest is the classic, most straightforward trigger for automatic disqualification; Pinochet (No 2) extended the same underlying principle to a non-pecuniary interest closely tied to the case. Either way, a fair-minded and informed observer would very likely see a real possibility of bias here.

testPool.prompt: A housing association's allocations panel refuses a tenant's transfer request. The panel chair is the line manager of the tenant's estranged partner, a fact known to the panel but not disclosed to the tenant. The tenant is not given a hearing, written or oral, before the decision. The refusal letter gives no reasons beyond 'request declined per policy'. Analyse the procedural fairness of the decision.
factsToOrder: The chair is the line manager of the tenant's estranged partner
This connection is known to the panel but not disclosed to the tenant
The tenant is given no hearing, written or oral
The refusal letter gives no reasons beyond 'request declined per policy'

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the panel's decision is unlawful for procedural impropriety on grounds of bias, denial of a hearing, and failure to give reasons.
modelAnswer.rule: Apparent bias is assessed by asking whether a fair-minded and informed observer would find a real possibility of bias (Porter v Magill); an undisclosed personal connection to a party strengthens that finding. Natural justice requires that a person facing a decision seriously affecting their interests be given notice and an opportunity to respond (Ridge v Baldwin). A common law duty to give reasons arises where fairness demands it, including where the decision would otherwise be inscrutable (ex p Doody).
modelAnswer.application: The chair's undisclosed connection to the tenant's estranged partner is precisely the kind of personal link a fair-minded and informed observer would see as raising a real possibility of bias, and the non-disclosure compounds the problem. Giving the tenant no hearing at all, written or oral, before a decision affecting their housing falls short of even the baseline standard set in Ridge v Baldwin. Finally, 'request declined per policy' gives no insight into the panel's actual reasoning, is inscrutable in the Doody sense, and prevents any meaningful challenge.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The decision is vulnerable on three independent grounds — apparent bias, denial of any hearing, and inadequate reasons — reinforcing each other and making the decision strongly likely to be quashed.

testPool.prompt: A council consults on a planning policy, discloses the alternatives it considered, genuinely reads all responses, and changes the final policy in response to feedback. Is this consultation likely to satisfy the Moseley standard?
options: Yes — this is close to the model of a fair consultation exercise
No — a consultation is only ever a formality regardless of how it is run

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is spotting one procedural defect in a fact pattern and stopping there. Strong answers run the full checklist — hearing, oral hearing, reasons, consultation, bias — against every fact pattern, because examiners routinely stack more than one head into a single problem.
